etymologies.etymologyHTML: Recorded since c. 1374 (displacing Old English toliesan) as Middle English dissolven, from Latin dissolvere (“to loosen up, break apart”) but with the sense from Anglo-Norman dissoldre (variant of Old French dissoudre), itself from dis- (“apart”) + solvere (“to loose, loosen”). By surface analysis, dis- +‎ solve.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To terminate a union of multiple members actively, as by disbanding.
(transitive) To liquify, melt into a fluid.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: as if the world were all dissolved to tears

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be melted, changed into a fluid.
(physical chemistry) (transitive) To disintegrate chemically into a solution by immersion into a liquid or other material.
(physical chemistry) (intransitive) To be disintegrated by such immersion.
(transitive) To disperse, drive apart a group of persons.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To break the continuity of; to disconnect; to loosen; to undo; to separate.

definitions.definition: (law, transitive) To annul; to rescind; to discharge or release.

definitions.definition: (cinematography, intransitive) To shift from one shot to another by having the former fade out as the latter fades in.
(intransitive) To resolve itself as by dissolution.
(obsolete) To solve; to clear up; to resolve.
